claims.source: One of the first examples of short-term deprivation in adults is by Mon-Williams et al., 1998, who found that thirty minutes of simulated myopia (optical blur achieved by wearing a +1D lens) was followed by a transient improvement of visual acuity – opposite to the long-lasting acuity deficit produced by early onset myopia (Rossi et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Contrast attenuation for 4 hr leads to improved contrast discrimination thresholds and enhanced BOLD response in V1/V2.
claims.source: Contrast attenuation for 4 hr leads to improved contrast discrimination thresholds and enhanced BOLD response in V1/V2 (Kwon et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: A few hours deprivation of one cardinal orientation leads to enhanced sensitivity to the deprived orientation.
claims.source: A few hours deprivation of one cardinal orientation leads to enhanced sensitivity to the deprived orientation (Zhang et al., 2009) – opposite to the reduced sensitivity to orientations deprived during development, for example due to astigmatism.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Two hours of monocular contrast deprivation is followed by a transient boost of the deprived eye.
claims.source: Similarly, two hours of monocular contrast deprivation is followed by a transient boost of the deprived eye (Binda and Lunghi, 2017; Lunghi et al., 2015a; Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2013; Lunghi et al., 2015b; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014) and an enlargement of the deprived-eye representation at the level of V1 in non-human primates (Begum and Tso, 2016; Tso et al., 2017) – opposite to the amblyopia induced by monocular deprivation during the critical period.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Two hours of monocular contrast deprivation leads to an enlargement of the deprived-eye representation at the level of V1 in non-human primates.
claims.source: Similarly, two hours of monocular contrast deprivation is followed by a transient boost of the deprived eye (Binda and Lunghi, 2017; Lunghi et al., 2015a; Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2013; Lunghi et al., 2015b; Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014) and an enlargement of the deprived-eye representation at the level of V1 in non-human primates (Begum and Tso, 2016; Tso et al., 2017) – opposite to the amblyopia induced by monocular deprivation during the critical period.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The mechanism supporting the perceptual boost of the deprived information could be either a form of homeostatic plasticity or a release of contrast adaptation for the deprived stimulus.
claims.source: The mechanism supporting the perceptual boost of the deprived information could be either a form of homeostatic plasticity (like that observed in animal models), and/or a release of contrast adaptation for the deprived stimulus (Blakemore and Campbell, 1969; Boynton et al., 1999; Gardner et al., 2005; Maffei et al., 1973; Movshon and Lennie, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Effects of short-term deprivation can be long-lasting or even permanent.
claims.source: Irrespective of the interpretation, the data clearly indicate that effects can be long-lasting or even permanent.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement based on inference from various studies.

claims.claim: In patients with keratoconus, best corrected visual acuity is worse than in emmetropic eyes, but it is better than predicted by the corneal dystrophy.
claims.source: For example, in patients with keratoconus (adult-onset corneal dystrophia, often monocular), best corrected visual acuity is worse than in emmetropic eyes, but it is better than predicted by the corneal dystrophy (Sabesan and Yoon, 2009; Sabesan and Yoon, 2010): when corneal aberrations of the keratoconic (KC) eyes are simulated in the emmetropic eyes, visual acuity is worse than in the KC eyes, demonstrating a permanent perceptual boost of the deprived information.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: When corneal aberrations of keratoconic eyes are simulated in emmetropic eyes, visual acuity is worse than in the keratoconic eyes, demonstrating a permanent perceptual boost of the deprived information.
claims.source: For example, in patients with keratoconus (adult-onset corneal dystrophia, often monocular), best corrected visual acuity is worse than in emmetropic eyes, but it is better than predicted by the corneal dystrophy (Sabesan and Yoon, 2009; Sabesan and Yoon, 2010): when corneal aberrations of the keratoconic (KC) eyes are simulated in the emmetropic eyes, visual acuity is worse than in the KC eyes, demonstrating a permanent perceptual boost of the deprived information.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research and inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: In adult amblyopes, short-term monocular deprivation (of the amblyopic eye) may lead to permanent partial recovery of acuity (of the amblyopic eye).
claims.source: Moreover, in adult amblyopes (Lunghi et al., 2018), short-term monocular deprivation (of the amblyopic eye) may lead to permanent partial recovery of acuity (of the amblyopic eye).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Homeostatic plasticity and Hebbian plasticity may be fundamentally linked.
claims.source: This observation resonates with the idea – introduced in the context of work at the cellular level – that homeostatic plasticity and Hebbian plasticity may be fundamentally linked (Maffei and Turrigiano, 2008) and may open important new pathways for the therapy of amblyopia and, in general, for the rehabilitation of early-onset visual dysfunctions (Legge and Chung, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited research.

claims.claim: Monocular deprivation effects have been indirectly studied with MR spectroscopy showing a GABA concentration change in the occipital cortex.
claims.source: So far, monocular deprivation effects have been indirectly studied with MR spectroscopy (showing a GABA concentration change in the occipital cortex, Lunghi et al., 2015b) and Visual Evoked Potentials (showing a modulation of the early visual response components, Lunghi et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Monocular deprivation effects have been indirectly studied with Visual Evoked Potentials showing a modulation of the early visual response components.
claims.source: So far, monocular deprivation effects have been indirectly studied with MR spectroscopy (showing a GABA concentration change in the occipital cortex, Lunghi et al., 2015b) and Visual Evoked Potentials (showing a modulation of the early visual response components, Lunghi et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Deprivation effects are not generalized but preferentially involve the parvocellular pathway.
claims.source: Indirect evidence also indicates that deprivation effects are not generalized but preferentially involve the parvocellular pathway – given that effects are more prominent and longer-lasting for chromatic equiluminant stimuli in humans (Lunghi et al., 2013), and strongest in macaques when deprivation mainly affects the parvocellular activity (Begum and Tso, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on cited research.

claims.claim: Effects of monocular deprivation are more prominent and longer-lasting for chromatic equiluminant stimuli in humans.
claims.source: Indirect evidence also indicates that deprivation effects are not generalized but preferentially involve the parvocellular pathway – given that effects are more prominent and longer-lasting for chromatic equiluminant stimuli in humans (Lunghi et al., 2013), and strongest in macaques when deprivation mainly affects the parvocellular activity (Begum and Tso, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Effects of monocular deprivation are strongest in macaques when deprivation mainly affects the parvocellular activity.
claims.source: Indirect evidence also indicates that deprivation effects are not generalized but preferentially involve the parvocellular pathway – given that effects are more prominent and longer-lasting for chromatic equiluminant stimuli in humans (Lunghi et al., 2013), and strongest in macaques when deprivation mainly affects the parvocellular activity (Begum and Tso, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The study directly measures the changes in early visual cortical areas using 7T fMRI in adult humans, before and after two hours of monocular deprivation.
claims.source: Here we directly measure the changes in early visual cortical areas using 7T fMRI in adult humans, before and after two hours of monocular deprivation.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claims.claim: The study demonstrates a change of ocular drive of BOLD signals in primary visual cortex, selective for the higher spatial frequencies and strongest along the ventral pathway.
claims.source: Assessing the BOLD change and its selectivity to spatial frequency with a newly developed approach (conceptually similar to the population Receptive Field method, Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008), we demonstrate a change of ocular drive of BOLD signals in primary visual cortex, selective for the higher spatial frequencies and strongest along the ventral pathway, consistent with a stronger plasticity potential of the parvocellular pathway in adulthood.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The change of ocular drive of BOLD signals is consistent with a stronger plasticity potential of the parvocellular pathway in adulthood.
claims.source: Assessing the BOLD change and its selectivity to spatial frequency with a newly developed approach (conceptually similar to the population Receptive Field method, Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008), we demonstrate a change of ocular drive of BOLD signals in primary visual cortex, selective for the higher spatial frequencies and strongest along the ventral pathway, consistent with a stronger plasticity potential of the parvocellular pathway in adulthood.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The V1 response to the high spatial frequency stimuli presented in the left and right eye is nearly equal before deprivation.
claims.source: Figure 1D shows that the V1 response to the high spatial frequency stimuli presented in the left and right eye is nearly equal before deprivation ('PRE')
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: After deprivation, the response in the two eyes changes in opposite directions, with a boost of the BOLD response of the deprived eye and a suppression of the non-deprived eye.
claims.source: However, after deprivation ('POST'), the response in the two eyes changes in opposite directions, with a boost of the BOLD response (measured as GLM Beta values, expressed in units of % signal change) of the deprived eye and a suppression of the non-deprived eye
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and related figures.

claims.claim: There is a significant interaction between the factors time (PRE, POST deprivation) and eye (deprived, non-deprived) for V1 BOLD responses to high spatial frequency stimuli.
claims.source: The result reveals a significant interaction between the factors time (PRE, POST deprivation) and eye (deprived, non-deprived; interaction term F(1,18) = 13.80703, p = 0.00158; the result survives a split-half reliability test: see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Before deprivation, the Ocular Dominance index is symmetrically distributed around zero, indicating a balanced representation of the two eyes.
claims.source: Before deprivation, the Ocular Dominance index is symmetrically distributed around zero, indicating a balanced representation of the two eyes before deprivation (yellow distribution in Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: After deprivation, the Ocular Dominance distribution shifts to the right of 0, indicating a preference for the deprived eye.
claims.source: After deprivation (black distribution in Figure 1E), the Ocular Dominance distribution shifts to the right of 0, indicating a preference for the deprived eye (non-parametric Wilcoxon sign-rank test comparing the PRE and POST Ocular Dominance medians, z = 115.39, p < 0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The shift of the Ocular Dominance histogram implies a recruitment of cortical resources for the representation of the deprived eye.
claims.source: The shift of the Ocular Dominance histogram in Figure 1E is more compatible with the latter case, implying a recruitment of cortical resources for the representation of the deprived eye.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed data pattern.

claims.claim: Vertices that originally preferred the deprived eye continue to prefer the same eye before and after deprivation.
claims.source: The majority of vertices continue to prefer the same eye before and after deprivation. The median Ocular Dominance is significantly larger than 0 both PRE and POST (Wilcoxon sign-rank test, z > 101.54, p < 0.0001 in both cases) and the correlation between Ocular Dominance indices before and after deprivation is strong and positive (Pearson's R(32236) = 0.22 [0.21–0.23], p < 0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Vertices originally preferring the deprived eye were largely unaffected by monocular deprivation.
claims.source: In addition, the distribution of Ocular Dominance after deprivation is well predicted by adding only a small amount of noise to the original half distribution (Gaussian noise with 0.12 standard deviation, black line), suggesting that these vertices were largely unaffected by monocular deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on modeling of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: For vertices originally preferring the non-deprived eye, there is a shift of Ocular Dominance with short term monocular deprivation.
claims.source: Contrary to Figure 2B, the POST- Ocular Dominance distribution cannot be predicted by injecting Gaussian noise to the PRE- Ocular Dominance distribution (black line, 0.12 standard deviation like for Figure 2B): for these vertices, there is a shift of Ocular Dominance with short term monocular deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and modeling analysis.

claims.claim: POST-deprivation BOLD responses to the deprived eye are significantly larger than POST-deprivation responses to the non-deprived eye in vertices originally preferring the non-deprived eye.
claims.source: In addition and crucially, POST-deprivation BOLD responses to the deprived eye are significantly larger than POST-deprivation responses to the non-deprived eye (t(18) = −2.775 p = 0.012; whereas, by selection, the opposite is true before deprivation: t(18) = 12.034, p < 10−5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Ocular Dominance before deprivation defines two similarly sized sub-regions of V1 vertices with radically different behaviors.
claims.source: In summary, Ocular Dominance before deprivation defines two similarly sized sub-regions of V1 vertices (44.58 ± 5.38% and 55.42 ± 5.38% of analyzed V1 vertices; 44.84 ± 5.12% and 55.16 ± 5.12% of all V1 vertices) with radically different behaviors that are not consistent with an artifact induced by vertex selection.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the data analysis results.

claims.claim: Short-term monocular contrast deprivation induced a 30% increase of phase duration for the deprived eye.
claims.source: In line with previous studies (Binda and Lunghi, 2017; Lunghi et al., 2015a; Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2015b; Lunghi and Sale, 2015), short-term monocular contrast deprivation induced a 30% increase of phase duration for the deprived eye (POST to PRE-deprivation ratio: 1.31 ± 0.30) and a 15% decrease of phase duration for the non-deprived eye (ratio: 0.86 ± 0.30), producing a significant time × eye interaction (Figure 3A, repeated measure ANOVA on the mean phase durations for each participant, interaction: F(1,18) = 23.56957, p = 0.00013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Short-term monocular contrast deprivation induced a 15% decrease of phase duration for the non-deprived eye.
claims.source: In line with previous studies (Binda and Lunghi, 2017; Lunghi et al., 2015a; Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2015b; Lunghi and Sale, 2015), short-term monocular contrast deprivation induced a 30% increase of phase duration for the deprived eye (POST to PRE-deprivation ratio: 1.31 ± 0.30) and a 15% decrease of phase duration for the non-deprived eye (ratio: 0.86 ± 0.30), producing a significant time × eye interaction (Figure 3A, repeated measure ANOVA on the mean phase durations for each participant, interaction: F(1,18) = 23.56957, p = 0.00013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The prolonged high contrast stimulation delivered for retinotopic mapping to the non-deprived eye during the first ~30 min of deprivation did not modulate the deprivation effects.
claims.source: This effect size is similar to that measured in recent experiments using the same paradigm, but letting subjects continue normal activity during the 2 hr of monocular deprivation (Lunghi et al., 2011; Lunghi et al., 2015b; Lunghi and Sale, 2015). This indicates that the prolonged high contrast stimulation delivered for retinotopic mapping to the non-deprived eye during the first ~30 min of deprivation did not modulate the deprivation effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with previous studies.

claims.claim: There is a strong correlation between the effect of monocular deprivation on psychophysics and BOLD.
claims.source: Using the same Equation 6 to compute the deprivation effect on BOLD responses (DIBOLD), we observed a strong correlation between the effect of monocular deprivation on psychophysics and BOLD (shown in Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Subjects who showed a strong deprivation effect at psychophysics also showed a strong deprivation effect in BOLD responses.
claims.source: Subjects who showed a strong deprivation effect at psychophysics (DIpsycho >2) also showed a strong deprivation effect in BOLD responses (DIBOLD = 1.85 ± 0.42).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The psychophysical effect may be used as a reliable proxy of a general change of cortical excitability, which can be measured by fMRI.
claims.source: Given that the psychophysics was measured only for central vision and at two cpd stationary grating, whereas BOLD responses were pooled across a large portion on V1 and were elicited using broadband dynamic stimuli, the correlation suggests that the psychophysical effect may be used as a reliable proxy of a general change of cortical excitability, which can be measured by fMRI.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed correlation.

claims.claim: The plasticity effect is absent at low spatial frequencies.
claims.source: In contrast with the strong and reliable plasticity of responses to the high spatial frequency stimulus (peaking at 2.7 cpd, Figures 1–3), we find that the plasticity effect is absent at low spatial frequencies (interaction index for the highest spatial frequency stimulus: 0.70 ± 0.19; for the lowest spatial frequency stimulus: 0.16 ± 0.15; paired t-test t(18) = −3.441, p = 0.003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Monocular deprivation produces a change of the spatial frequency selectivity of the V1 BOLD response.
claims.source: Thus, monocular deprivation produces a change of the spatial frequency selectivity of the V1 BOLD response.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Before deprivation, the BOLD response shows a broad band-pass selectivity for stimuli, with a preference for the stimulus peaking at intermediate spatial frequencies, between 0.4 and 1.1 cpd.
claims.source: Before deprivation, the BOLD response shows a broad band-pass selectivity for our stimuli, with a preference for the stimulus peaking at intermediate spatial frequencies, between 0.4 and 1.1 cpd, and a slight attenuation at higher spatial frequencies, similar for the two eyes (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: After deprivation, the non-deprived eye shows similar selectivity and an overall decrease of responses.
claims.source: After deprivation (Figure 4B), the non-deprived eye shows similar selectivity and an overall decrease of responses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: After deprivation, for the deprived eye, the shape of the spatial frequency tuning curve changes from band-pass to high-pass.
claims.source: For the deprived eye, the shape of the curve changes: from band-pass to high-pass, implying that the enhancement affects primarily the higher spatial frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The enhancement after deprivation affects primarily the higher spatial frequencies.
claims.source: For the deprived eye, the shape of the curve changes: from band-pass to high-pass, implying that the enhancement affects primarily the higher spatial frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed change in spatial frequency tuning.

claims.claim: The spatial frequency cut-off is around 16 in the para-fovea (eccentricity around 1.5 deg) and down to four in the periphery (eccentricity around 8 deg).
claims.source: The cut-off is around 16 in the para-fovea (eccentricity around 1.5 deg) and down to four in the periphery (eccentricity around 8 deg).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The relationship between eccentricity and spatial frequency preference is consistent with previous fMRI results and with psychophysics.
claims.source: This relationship between eccentricity and spatial frequency preference is consistent with previous fMRI results (D'Souza et al., 2016; Henriksson et al., 2008) and with psychophysics (Rovamo et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited previous research.

claims.claim: For the non-deprived eye, there is no effect of deprivation on spatial frequency selectivity.
claims.source: For the non-deprived eye, there is no effect of deprivation on spatial frequency selectivity (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: For the deprived eye, there is a shift towards preferring higher spatial frequencies, at all eccentricities.
claims.source: In contrast, for the deprived eye (Figure 5D), there is a shift towards preferring higher spatial frequencies, at all eccentricities, which is captured by an increased value of the cut-off frequency parameter leading to an increased acuity of the BOLD response to the deprived eye.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The change of spatial frequency selectivity for the deprived eye is most evident at eccentricities of 4 deg and higher.
claims.source: Note that the change of spatial frequency selectivity for the deprived eye is most evident at eccentricities of 4 deg and higher (see Figure 5D), where vertices have peak sensitivity at mid-to-low spatial frequencies before deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The spatial frequency selectivity for the non-deprived eye is unchanged at all eccentricities.
claims.source: Importantly, the spatial frequency selectivity for the non-deprived eye is unchanged at all eccentricities, corroborating the eye and stimulus specificity of the short-term monocular deprivation effect.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data analysis.

claims.claim: The increase of spatial frequency cut-off for the deprived eye is significant.
claims.source: This is clarified by post-hoc t-tests revealing that the increase of spatial frequency cut-off for the deprived eye is significant (t(18) = −2.263, p = 0.036) whereas there is no significant change for the non-deprived eye (t(18) = 0.440, p = 0.665).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: POST-deprivation, the deprived eye shows an increase of mean phase duration (in binocular rivalry) and an increase of the spatial frequency cut-off (best fit of the BOLD responses).
claims.source: POST-deprivation, the deprived eye shows an increase of mean phase duration (in binocular rivalry) and an increase of the spatial frequency cut-off (best fit of the BOLD responses): participants showing a stronger increase of phase duration, also showed a larger shift of selectivity towards higher spatial frequency.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Participants showing a stronger increase of phase duration also showed a larger shift of selectivity towards higher spatial frequency.
claims.source: POST-deprivation, the deprived eye shows an increase of mean phase duration (in binocular rivalry) and an increase of the spatial frequency cut-off (best fit of the BOLD responses): participants showing a stronger increase of phase duration, also showed a larger shift of selectivity towards higher spatial frequency.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The selective boost of the deprived eye response to the high spatial frequency is as strong in V2 as in V1.
claims.source: The selective boost of the deprived eye response to the high spatial frequency is as strong in V2 as in V1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in the referenced figures.

claims.claim: The boost is present also in V3 and V4.
claims.source: The boost is present also in V3 and V4.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: In V4 the boost appears to be present also for lower spatial frequencies, but again only for the deprived eye.
claims.source: In V4 the boost appears to be present also for lower spatial frequencies, but again only for the deprived eye (Figure 7A–B), possibly reflecting the larger spatial frequency bandwidth of V4 neurons compared to V1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-B and inference about V4 neuron properties.

claims.claim: Dorsal area V3a does not show any significant change of responses in either eye at high spatial frequencies.
claims.source: The results are very different for dorsal area V3a (Figure 7C–D) and hMT+ (Figure 7E–F), which do not show any significant change of responses in either eye at high spatial frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claims.source: The results are very different for dorsal area V3a (Figure 7C–D) and hMT+ (Figure 7E–F), which do not show any significant change of responses in either eye at high spatial frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claims.claim: The plasticity effect is strongest in V1, V2 and V3.
claims.source: The plasticity effect is strongest in V1, V2 and V3; it is still strong and significant in ventral area V4 (t(18) = 2.41 p = 0.0270), but it is absent in V3a and hMT+, where the time x eye interaction is not significantly different from 0 (t(18) = 0.52 p = 0.6115 and t(18) = −0.19 p = 0.8513 respectively).

claims.claim: The plasticity effect is still strong and significant in ventral area V4.
claims.source: The plasticity effect is strongest in V1, V2 and V3; it is still strong and significant in ventral area V4 (t(18) = 2.41 p = 0.0270), but it is absent in V3a and hMT+, where the time x eye interaction is not significantly different from 0 (t(18) = 0.52 p = 0.6115 and t(18) = −0.19 p = 0.8513 respectively).

claims.claim: The plasticity effect is absent in V3a and hMT+.
claims.source: The plasticity effect is strongest in V1, V2 and V3; it is still strong and significant in ventral area V4 (t(18) = 2.41 p = 0.0270), but it is absent in V3a and hMT+, where the time x eye interaction is not significantly different from 0 (t(18) = 0.52 p = 0.6115 and t(18) = −0.19 p = 0.8513 respectively).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7G and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The plasticity effect in ventral area V4 is significantly stronger than in dorsal areas V3a and hMT+.
claims.source: The plasticity effect in ventral area V4 is significantly stronger than in dorsal areas V3a and hMT+ (t(18) = 2.39, p = 0.0278 and t(18) = 2.36, p = 0.0299 for V4-V3a and V4-hMT+ respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The differential plasticity effect in extra-striate visual areas of the ventral and dorsal pathway suggests a preferential involvement of the parvocellular vs. magnocellular pathway.
claims.source: This result suggests a preferential involvement of the parvocellular vs. magnocellular pathway, leading to the differential plasticity effect in extra-striate visual areas of the ventral and dorsal pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences between ventral and dorsal areas.

claims.claim: The plasticity effect is robust in areas where the majority of cells are binocular (like V3 and V4).
claims.source: Interestingly, the plasticity effect is robust in areas where the majority of cells are binocular (like V3 and V4), indicating that the effect does not require segregated representations of the two eyes (e.g. Ocular Dominance columns).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: The effect does not require segregated representations of the two eyes (e.g. Ocular Dominance columns).
claims.source: Interestingly, the plasticity effect is robust in areas where the majority of cells are binocular (like V3 and V4), indicating that the effect does not require segregated representations of the two eyes (e.g. Ocular Dominance columns).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Two hours of abnormal visual experience has a profound impact on the neural sensitivity and selectivity of V1.
claims.source: We demonstrate that two hours of abnormal visual experience has a profound impact on the neural sensitivity and selectivity of V1.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claims.claim: BOLD activity across the V1 cortical region paradoxically increases for the eye that was deprived of contrast vision, and decreases for the eye exposed to normal visual experience.
claims.source: BOLD activity across the V1 cortical region paradoxically increases for the eye that was deprived of contrast vision, and decreases for the eye exposed to normal visual experience.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the primary experimental findings.

claims.claim: The enhanced response to the deprived eye fits well with the concept of homeostatic plasticity, first observed in rodent visual cortex, both juvenile and adult.
claims.source: The enhanced response to the deprived eye fits well with the concept of homeostatic plasticity, first observed in rodent visual cortex, both juvenile and adult (Maffei et al., 2004; Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004), which is the tendency of neural circuits to keep the average firing rates constant in spite of anomalous stimulation (Maffei and Turrigiano, 2008; Turrigiano, 2012) (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Turrigiano and Nelson, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on cited research.

claims.claim: Similar observations of post-deprivation gain boost have been made in the adult macaque V1 after two hours of monocular deprivation during anesthesia.
claims.source: More recently, similar observations have been made in the adult macaque V1 after two hours of monocular deprivation during anesthesia (Begum and Tso, 2016; Tso et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The post-deprivation gain boost observed in the monkey is consistent with observations of an increased BOLD response to the deprived eye in humans.
claims.source: The post-deprivation gain boost observed in the monkey is consistent with our observations of an increased BOLD response to the deprived eye.
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings with previous research.

claims.claim: An antagonistic suppression of the non-deprived eye BOLD response is observed.
claims.source: We also observe an antagonistic suppression of the non-deprived eye BOLD response; together, the two effects lead to a shift of ocular preference of individual vertices in favor of the deprived eye.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Together, the boost of the deprived eye and suppression of the non-deprived eye lead to a shift of ocular preference of individual vertices in favor of the deprived eye.
claims.source: We also observe an antagonistic suppression of the non-deprived eye BOLD response; together, the two effects lead to a shift of ocular preference of individual vertices in favor of the deprived eye.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The shift of ocular preference is only observed in those V1 vertices that responded preferentially to the non-deprived eye before deprivation.
claims.source: However, this effect is only observed in those V1 vertices that responded preferentially to the non-deprived eye before deprivation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

results.result: Short-term (2 hr) monocular deprivation in adult humans boosts the BOLD response to the deprived eye and changes ocular dominance of V1 vertices. Before deprivation, V1 responses to high spatial frequency stimuli are balanced between eyes, but after deprivation, the deprived eye shows increased BOLD response while the non-deprived eye shows suppression, resulting in a significant time × eye interaction and a shift in the ocular dominance distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C50-C54, and C95 are well-supported by experimental fMRI data showing significant statistical effects (F(1,18) = 13.80703, p = 0.00158) and shifts in ocular dominance distributions (z = 115.39, p < 0.001). The findings are visualized in Figures 1 and 2 with appropriate controls and replication (split-half reliability test).

results.result: The shift in ocular dominance after deprivation is selective: vertices originally preferring the deprived eye remain unchanged, while vertices originally preferring the non-deprived eye shift their preference toward the deprived eye. This pattern suggests recruitment of cortical resources normally dedicated to the non-deprived eye rather than a general gain increase.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 and C100-C104 are supported by detailed analysis of vertex subpopulations shown in Figure 2, with strong statistical evidence (correlation R = 0.22, p < 0.0001; t-tests with p < 0.012). The modeling approach (adding Gaussian noise) provides additional validation that the effect is specific to vertices originally preferring the non-deprived eye.

results.result: Short-term monocular deprivation induces changes in binocular rivalry dynamics, with a 30% increase in phase duration for the deprived eye and a 15% decrease for the non-deprived eye. The effect size is similar to previous studies, indicating that retinotopic mapping stimulation during deprivation did not modulate the effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are supported by psychophysical measurements showing significant time × eye interaction (F(1,18) = 23.56957, p = 0.00013) and comparison with previous studies. The inference about lack of modulation from retinotopic mapping (C63) is reasonable based on effect size comparison but could benefit from direct experimental control.

results.result: The V1 deprivation effect correlates across participants with perceptual changes measured by binocular rivalry, suggesting a common origin. This correlation holds despite binocular rivalry being restricted to foveal vision while BOLD measurements span V1, indicating that binocular rivalry may serve as a proxy for general cortical plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C64-C66, and C109-C112 are supported by correlation data shown in Figure 3B (Pearson's correlation, p = 0.036). The inference that binocular rivalry serves as a proxy for general plasticity (C66, C112) is reasonable given the correlation, though the mechanistic link requires further validation. The correlation is meaningful despite different spatial extents of the measurements.

results.result: Monocular deprivation produces a change in spatial frequency selectivity of V1 BOLD responses, with the plasticity effect absent at low spatial frequencies but strong at high spatial frequencies. For the deprived eye, the spatial frequency tuning changes from band-pass to high-pass, indicating enhancement primarily affects higher spatial frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C67-C72 are supported by experimental data across five spatial frequency stimuli (Figures 4-5), with significant statistical differences (paired t-test t(18) = −3.441, p = 0.003). The characterization of tuning curve changes from band-pass to high-pass is well-documented in Figure 4B. The modeling approach using DoG functions provides quantitative support.

results.result: Spatial frequency cut-off varies with eccentricity (from ~16 cpd at 1.5 deg to ~4 cpd at 8 deg) in a manner consistent with previous fMRI and psychophysical studies. After deprivation, the deprived eye shows a significant shift toward higher spatial frequencies at all eccentricities, while the non-deprived eye remains unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C79 are supported by pRF modeling and spatial frequency tuning analysis shown in Figure 5, with significant post-hoc t-test for the deprived eye (t(18) = −2.263, p = 0.036) but not for the non-deprived eye (t(18) = 0.440, p = 0.665). The consistency with prior work (C74) strengthens confidence in the measurements.

results.result: The increase in spatial frequency cut-off for the deprived eye correlates with the increase in binocular rivalry phase duration across participants, with those showing stronger perceptual changes also showing larger shifts in spatial frequency selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C81 are supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B (R(19) = 0.68, p = 0.001). This cross-modal correlation between neural and perceptual measures strengthens the interpretation that both reflect a common plasticity mechanism.

results.result: The deprivation effect is strongest in V1, present in V2, V3, and V4, but absent in dorsal areas V3a and hMT+. The plasticity effect in ventral area V4 is significantly stronger than in dorsal areas V3a and hMT+, suggesting differential involvement of ventral versus dorsal visual pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C8 and C82-C90 are supported by systematic analysis across visual areas shown in Figure 7, with appropriate statistical tests (V4: t(18) = 2.41, p = 0.027; V3a: t(18) = 0.52, p = 0.61; hMT+: t(18) = −0.19, p = 0.85). The differential effects across areas are statistically significant (V4 vs V3a: t(18) = 2.39, p = 0.028).

results.result: The preferential boost of high spatial frequencies and stronger effects in ventral areas (V4) compared to dorsal areas (V3a, hMT+) suggest primary involvement of the parvocellular pathway, which preferentially processes high spatial frequencies and projects to ventral stream areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C91, C123-C125 represent reasonable inferences based on established knowledge about visual pathway organization and the experimental findings showing spatial frequency selectivity and ventral/dorsal differences. However, the study does not directly manipulate or measure parvocellular versus magnocellular activity, so this remains an inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: The observed BOLD changes are consistent with homeostatic plasticity, demonstrating that two hours of abnormally unbalanced visual experience induces functional reorganization of cortical circuits, particularly in the parvocellular pathway, leading to altered visual perceptual abilities. The visual cortex, particularly the ventral pathway, retains high potential for homeostatic plasticity in human adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C13, C94, C96, C98-C99, and C150-C151 represent interpretations of the experimental findings in the context of homeostatic plasticity theory. The interpretation is well-supported by the data showing paradoxical enhancement of the deprived eye (opposite to developmental deprivation effects) and consistency with animal studies. However, the mechanism is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: The plasticity effect is robust in areas where the majority of cells are binocular (V3 and V4), indicating that the effect does not require segregated representations of the two eyes such as ocular dominance columns.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by the observation of strong effects in V3 and V4 (Figure 7), which are known to have predominantly binocular cells. This is a reasonable inference based on established knowledge of visual area organization, though the study does not directly measure ocular dominance column structure.

results.result: The correlation between V1 deprivation effects and binocular rivalry suggests a common origin and could validate the use of binocular rivalry as a biomarker of adult cortical plasticity. Binocular rivalry originates in primary visual cortex and reflects excitatory-inhibitory dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claim C12 is supported by the observed correlation, but the inference of 'common origin' is speculative. Claims C113-C116 about binocular rivalry as a biomarker and its neural basis (C114-C116) are based on cited literature but represent future potential rather than demonstrated results. The validation of binocular rivalry as a biomarker would require additional prospective studies.

results.result: The study used 7T fMRI to directly measure changes in early visual cortical areas in 19 adult humans before and after 2 hours of monocular deprivation, demonstrating changes in ocular drive selective for higher spatial frequencies and strongest along the ventral pathway, consistent with parvocellular pathway involvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 and C152-C159 describe the experimental approach and are supported by the methods section. The sample size (n=19) was justified by power analysis for detecting correlations. The deprivation procedure using translucent patches is well-characterized and consistent with previous studies.

results.result: Background claims about critical period plasticity, developmental effects of monocular deprivation, homeostatic plasticity in animal models, and adult visual cortex plasticity are established from prior literature and provide context for the current study.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C14-C30 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide necessary context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Prior research has demonstrated various forms of short-term deprivation effects in adults, including paradoxical enhancement of deprived stimuli, with evidence suggesting preferential involvement of the parvocellular pathway and potential for long-lasting or permanent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C46 summarize prior research with appropriate citations. These establish the context and motivation for the current study but are not novel findings. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

results.result: Discussion claims connecting current findings to prior work on homeostatic plasticity in macaques, VEP studies, GABAergic mechanisms, perceptual learning, and potential for Hebbian plasticity outside the critical period.
results.evaluation: Claims C97, C105, C107-C108, C117-C122, C126-C129, C132-C137, and C140-C143 represent interpretations and connections to prior literature that are appropriately cited and provide reasonable context for the findings. These are not novel results but appropriate scholarly discussion.

results.result: Speculative claims about potential links between homeostatic and Hebbian plasticity, mechanisms underlying the effects, therapeutic implications for amblyopia, and potential for stable changes in adult cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C41, C106, C130-C131, C138-C139, and C144-C149 represent speculation about mechanisms and future implications. While these are reasonable hypotheses based on the data and prior literature, they are not directly tested in this study. Claims about therapeutic potential (C145-C149) are particularly speculative and would require clinical trials to validate.
